items.title: Relation between Angular and Linear Velocities

source_refs.note: Relation between Angular and Linear Velocities: a main subheading of 3.1 Angular measurements, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 54-54.

blocks.text: Consider a rigid body rotating about z-axis with an angular velocity ω as shown in Fig. 3.5 (a).

blocks.alt: A vertical z-axis with a curled arrow labelled ω near the top. A pink rigid body sticks out from O on the axis, with a dashed line r inside it from O to the point P.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.5(a): A rigid body rotating about the z-axis with angular velocity ω (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.5(a)).

blocks.text: Imagine a point P in the rigid body at a perpendicular distance r from the axis of rotation. OP represents the reference line of the rigid body. As the body rotates, the point P moves along a circle of radius r with a linear velocity v whereas the line OP rotates with angular velocity ω as shown in Fig. 3.5 (b). We are interested in finding out the relation between ω and v. As the axis of rotation is fixed, so the direction of ω always remains the same and ω can be manipulated as a scalar. As regards the linear velocity of the point P, we consider its magnitude only which can also be treated as a scalar.

blocks.alt: A horizontal circle drawn as an ellipse with centre O, a y-axis to the right, an x-axis towards the viewer and a z-axis upward carrying a thick blue arrow ω. Radii from O reach P₁ and P₂ on the front of the circle; OP₁ makes angle θ with the x-axis, the small angle between OP₁ and OP₂ is Δθ, and an arrow along the arc from P₁ to P₂ is labelled ΔS. OP₁ is labelled r.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.5(b): Point P moves through the arc P₁P₂ = ΔS while OP turns through Δθ (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.5(b)).

In the second, the wheel has turned through angle θ: B now touches the ground and A is up on the rim. blocks.title: Point to Ponder

blocks.text: In the limit when Δt → 0 the ratio ΔS/Δt represents v, the magnitude of the velocity with which point P is moving on the circumference of the circle. Similarly Δθ/Δt represents the angular velocity ω of the reference line OP. So, Eq. 3.6 becomes:

From Fig. 3.5(b), it can be seen that the point P is moving along the arc P₁P₂. In the limit when Δt → 0, the length of arc P₁P₂ becomes very small and its direction represents the direction of tangent to the circle at point P₁. Thus, the velocity with which point P is moving on the circumference of the circle has a magnitude v and its direction is always along the tangent to the circle at that point. That is why, the linear velocity of the point P is also known as tangential velocity.

Similarly, Eq. 3.7 shows that if the reference line OP is rotating with an angular acceleration α, the point P will also have a linear or tangential acceleration aₜ. Using Eq. 3.7 it can be shown that the two accelerations are related by

Eqs. 3.7 and 3.8 show that on a rotating body, points that are at different distances from the axis do not have the same speed or acceleration, but all points on a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis do have the same angular displacement, angular speed and angular acceleration at any instant. Thus, by the use of angular variables, we can describe the motion of the entire body in a simple way.
